drills.q: Explain precisely why Cloud Run scales to zero in a way Fargate doesn't, mechanically.
drills.a: Cloud Run's front door is an always-available request router that can hold an inbound request while launching a fresh instance on demand -- wake-on-request is a first-class platform feature. Fargate has no equivalent; reaching zero tasks requires explicit Auto Scaling config, and scaling back up needs an external trigger, with a cold path (ENI provisioning, image pull) of tens of seconds to minutes.

drills.q: A team's background job kicked off after returning an HTTP 200 keeps silently stopping partway through on Cloud Run. Diagnose.
drills.a: The default 'CPU only allocated during request processing' mode throttles CPU to near-zero once no request is in-flight, starving detached background work left running after the response. Fix: await the work before responding, offload to Cloud Tasks/Pub/Sub, or explicitly switch to 'CPU always allocated' for that service.

drills.q: Compare Cloud Functions 1st gen and 2nd gen concurrency models and the cost/performance consequence.
drills.a: 1st gen: exactly one request per instance -- every concurrent request needs its own instance. 2nd gen (built on Cloud Run) supports true per-instance concurrency up to 1,000 for I/O-bound workloads, so bursty traffic can run on far fewer instances. Consequence: materially different cost and cold-start-exposure profiles under load.

drills.q: When would you choose GKE Autopilot over Cloud Run for a workload that's still mostly stateless services?
drills.a: Once it needs arbitrary long-lived non-HTTP TCP protocols, sidecar generality beyond Cloud Run's limits, StatefulSet-style stable identity/persistent storage, or fine-grained custom scheduling -- Cloud Run doesn't support these natively; GKE Autopilot keeps the no-node-management simplicity while adding full Kubernetes generality.

drills.q: Explain the difference between a direct Eventarc event and an audit-log-derived event and why it matters operationally.
drills.a: Direct events are emitted natively via a purpose-built stream from ~100+ first-party GCP sources, low latency. Audit-log-derived events are sourced from Cloud Audit Logs -- much broader coverage (any API call on any resource) but can lag a real direct event for the same action since they're sourced from a logging pipeline, not a dedicated event stream. Prefer direct events whenever available.

drills.q: Design Cloud Run configuration for a payment API that cannot tolerate cold starts vs an internal webhook receiver that can.
drills.a: Payment API: minScale >= 2, concurrency tuned to actual per-request CPU cost, 'CPU always allocated' only if genuine background work must survive past the response. Webhook receiver: minScale: 0 is fine, higher concurrency (I/O-bound), default CPU allocation mode -- occasional cold starts on an internal path are invisible.

drills.q: How would you estimate whether a spiky, low-average-traffic internal service is cheaper on Cloud Run or Fargate?
drills.a: Cloud Run costs roughly (vCPU-seconds actually consumed + memory-seconds consumed) x rate + per-request charge, billed in 100ms increments, with zero cost during idle windows. Fargate costs (provisioned vCPU/memory x hours running) x rate, billed continuously regardless of traffic, unless Auto Scaling actively reduces task count (and even then, zero means giving up availability during the cold-start-back-up window). Long idle stretches favor Cloud Run; steady high utilization narrows the gap.

drills.q: Why did Google rebuild Cloud Functions 2nd gen on top of Cloud Run rather than maintaining a separate execution engine?
drills.a: To converge scaling and cold-start engineering into one shared runtime so every Cloud Run improvement automatically benefits Cloud Run functions, while keeping the lighter function-first deployment experience as a product-level differentiator rather than duplicating infrastructure across two engines with a strictly worse concurrency/timeout story for Functions users.

drills.q: Design an event-driven pipeline: file upload triggers virus scan, then thumbnail generation, then a database update, each independently scalable and retryable.
drills.a: Cloud Storage object-finalize emits a direct Eventarc event to a virus-scan Cloud Run function. On success it publishes to Pub/Sub (decoupling from the next stage's availability) which triggers a thumbnail-generation Cloud Run service via an Eventarc Pub/Sub trigger, which itself publishes completion for a final function to update the database. Each stage gets independent retry policy, dead-letter topic, and scaling tuning -- a failure downstream doesn't cascade upstream.

drills.q: Does setting minScale >= 1 on Cloud Run guarantee zero cold starts under all traffic patterns?
drills.a: No. It guarantees warm instances are always available for baseline traffic, but a sudden spike beyond what those warm instances can handle at the configured concurrency still triggers new cold-start instances for the overflow -- minScale reduces cold-start frequency, it doesn't eliminate cold starts during scale-out events.
